chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Husayn from Ibn Muskān from Abū 'Ubaydah said:

I heard Abū Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) would, when it was a dark night with wind and rain, pray Maghrib, then remain for the time it takes for people to perform voluntary prayers, then his muezzin would call the Adhan, then he would pray the final 'Isha', then they would depart.'

And the second [ruling] is that it is a concession for entering the prayer for one who knows that the twilight will fall before he finishes the prayer, because whenever the matter is as we described, it suffices him. And there is nothing in these narrations indicating that it is permissible for him to pray before the twilight falls, even if he knows he will finish while the twilight remains. So if what we mentioned can be interpreted that way, we interpret it as such. And that which indicates that this is permissible is what he narrated:

key_terms.اَلشَّفَقُ: Twilight (the reddish glow in the sky after sunset)
key_terms.رُخْصَةً: Concession or dispensation in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: What is the Prophet's practice for combining Maghrib and Isha prayers during bad weather?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Prophet’s (peace be upon him) practical flexibility in combining Maghrib and 'Isha prayers during adverse weather, a practice later expanded by Shia jurists to include 'Asr and Maghrib. It clarifies the distinction between the primary Sunnah of waiting for full twilight disappearance and the legal concession (rukhsah) allowing prayer to begin if one is certain it will conclude before the time ends, reflecting the Shia emphasis on ease within ritual precision. This principle underscores the balance between strict adherence to prayer times and accommodating the congregation's comfort during inclement conditions.
